chunks: "Resistance is how much a piece of material opposes current flow. Operationally it's the ratio of the voltage across it to the current through it, R equals V over I, in ohms.
One ohm is one volt per amp.

Physically, when you apply a voltage you create an electric field that accelerates the free electrons, but they keep scattering off lattice vibrations, impurities and defects, so instead of accelerating forever they reach a steady average drift speed.
The more they scatter, the more voltage you need for the same current, so the higher the resistance.
All that scattering turns electrical energy into heat, which is why current through a resistance dissipates I squared R.
For a uniform conductor, resistance is rho times length over area, where rho is the material's resistivity. Doubling the length doubles it, doubling the cross section halves it.
Copper is about 1. 7 times ten to the minus eight ohm-meters, glass is more than ten orders of magnitude higher.
And it's worth saying that V over I is a definition, while Ohm's law is the observation that for many materials this ratio is constant.
A diode or a lamp filament has a V over I that changes with the operating point."
